title: Definition
body_md: The $n^{th}$ Temperley-Lieb algebra $TL_n$ is the free $\mathbb{Z}[A, A^{-1}]$-module generated by all $(n,n)$-planar tangle diagrams, with the relation $\bigcirc = -A^2 - A^{-2}$. The multiplication in $TL_n$ is induced by concatenating $(n,n)$-planar tangles.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: The trace map on $TL_n$ is the $\mathbb{Z}[A, A^{-1}]$-module homomorphism $tr: TL_n \to TL_0$, induced by taking closures of $(n,n)$-planar tangles.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: The Jones representation of the braid group $Br_n$ is the monoid homomorphism $J_n: Br_n \to TL_n$ sending $\sigma_i$ to $A (id_n) + A^{-1} e_i$, sending $\sigma_i^{-1}$ to $A^{-1}(id_n) + A e_i$.

label: def:jones-polynomial
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:jones-polynomial}
    Let $b$ be a braid in $Br_n$. Define the Jones polynomial of $b$ to be the Laurent polynomial
    $$
    V_b(q) = (-1)^{|b|+1} q^{\frac{3w(b)}{2}}\frac{\langle b \rangle(q^{-\frac{1}{2}})}{q+q^{-1}} \in \mathbb{Z}[q, q^{-1}]
    $$
    where $|b|$ is the length of any braid word of $b$, and $w(b)$ is the writhe of the corresponding oriented tangle diagram. By the braid relations, $(-1)^{|b|+1}$ and $w(b)$ are both well-defined.

label: s.d. interval and partition
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{s.d. interval and partition}
	A standard dyadic interval (s.d. interval) is an interval of the form $[\frac{k}{2^m}, \frac{k+1}{2^m}]$ for some $m \in \{0,1,2,...\}$ and $k \in \{0,1,2,...,2^m-1\}$. A standard dyadic partition (s.d. partition) on $[0,1]$ is a finite partition $\{0 = a_0 < a_1 < ... < a_n = 1\}$ such that $[a_i, a_{i+1}]$ is an s.d. interval for all $i$.

	We call $a_i$ a breakpoint of the s.d. partition, and call $[a_i, a_{i+1}]$ a subinterval of the s.d. partition. A standard dyadic partition with $n$ subintervals is called a standard dyadic $n$-partition (s.d. $n$-partition). Suppose $\mathcal{K}$ and $\mathcal{I}$ are s.d. partitions, we denote $\mathcal{K} \leq \mathcal{I}$ if $\mathcal{I}$ is a refinement of $\mathcal{K}$ as partitions. In other words, the set of breakpoints of $\mathcal{K}$ is a subset of the set of breakpoints of $\mathcal{I}$.

    Let $\mathfrak{T}$ denote the set of all standard dyadic partitions, then $(\mathfrak{T}, \leq)$ is an ordered set.

title: Definition
body_md:
Given $(\mathcal{C},\sim)$, a category with concentration, define the \textbf{concentration monoid} of $(\mathcal{C}, \sim)$ to be $M_{(\mathcal{C}, \sim)} = \textup{Mor}_{\mathcal{C}} / \sim$, with multiplication 
    $$
    [f][g] = [f' \circ g']
    $$
    where $f' \sim f, g' \sim g$ and $f' \circ g'$ exists. The third axiom of concentration structure guarantees that we can always find such $f'$ and $g'$.

body_md: Suppose that $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{D}$ are categories with $G$-actions on them. Let $F_1, F_2$ be two $G$-equivariant functors from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{D}$. We say a natural transformation $\tau$ from $F_1$ to $F_2$ is $G$-equivariant if $g(\tau_A) = \tau_{g(A)}$ for any $g \in G$ and any object $A$ in $\mathcal{C}$.

label: prop:S-functor-induces-SG-functor
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:S-functor-induces-SG-functor}
    Let $\mathcal{S}$ and $\mathcal{S}'$ be two direct categories with $G$-actions on them, and let $F, \ F'$ be two $G$-equivariant functors from $\mathcal{S}, \ \mathcal{S}'$ to $\mathcal{M}on$ respectively (recall that we always require that $G$ acts trivially on $\mathcal{M}on$). Then given any $G$-equivariant functor $\rho:\mathcal{S} \rightarrow\mathcal{S}'$, and a $G$-equivariant natural transformation $\tau$ from $F$ to $F' \circ \rho$, $\rho$ and $\tau$ induce a concentration preserving functor
    $$
    \rho_\tau: (\mathcal{S}_G, \sim) \to (\mathcal{S}'_G, \sim')
    $$
    sending object $A$ to $\rho(A)$, morphism $(A, \alpha, f)$ to $(\rho(A), \tau_A(\alpha), f)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first check that $\rho_\tau$ is a well-defined functor. Suppose that $(A, \alpha, f)$ is a morphism from $B$ to $A$, then $\rho_\tau(A, \alpha, f) = (\rho(A), \tau_A(\alpha), f)$ is indeed a morphism from $\rho(B)$ to $\rho(A)$, since $\rho$ is $G$-equivariant we have $f(\rho(B)) = \rho(f(B)) = \rho(A)$. It is easy to see that $\rho_\tau$ preserves identity morphisms, since $\tau_A$ is a monoid homomorphism for any $A$. Now given another morphism                                       
    $(B, \beta, g)$ from $C$ to $B$, we have
    \begin{align*}
        \rho_\tau(A, \alpha, f) \circ \rho_\tau(B, \beta, g) 
        &= (\rho(A), \tau_A(\alpha), f) \circ (\rho(B), \tau_B(\beta), g) \\
        &= (\rho(A), \tau_A(\alpha)\tau_B(\beta), fg) \\
        &= (\rho(A), \tau_A(\alpha)\tau_A(\beta), fg) \\
        &= (\rho(A), \tau_A(\alpha\beta), fg) \\
        &= \rho_\tau(A, \alpha\beta, fg) \\
        &= \rho_\tau((A, \alpha, f) \circ (B, \beta, g))
    \end{align*}
 where from line $2$ to line $3$ we use the fact that $\tau$ is $G$-equivariant, hence $\tau_A(\beta)=\tau_{f(B)}(\beta)=f(\tau_B(\beta))=\tau_B(\beta)$.

    Then we check that $\rho_\tau$ preserves the concentration structures. Suppose that $(A, \alpha, f) \sim (B, \beta, g)$, then $f = g$ and there exists some $C \geq A, B$ such that $(F(\iota_A^C))(\alpha) = (F(\iota_B^C))(\beta)$, and we want to show $(\rho(A),
    \tau_A(\alpha),f) \sim' (\rho(B),
    \tau_B(\beta),f)$. By definition it is enough to show $(F'(\iota_{\rho(A)}^{\rho(C)}))(\tau_A(\alpha))=(F'(\iota_{\rho(B)}^{\rho(C)}))(\tau_B(\beta))$ which follows from the following two commutative diagrams on the naturality.

    \[\begin{tikzcd}
    	{F(C)} & {F'(\rho(C))} &&& {F(C)} & {F'(\rho(C))} \\
    	{F(A)} & {F'(\rho(A))} &&& {F(B)} & {F'(\rho(B))}
    	\arrow["{\tau_C}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
    	\arrow["{\tau_C}", from=1-5, to=1-6]
    	\arrow["{F(\iota_A^C)}", from=2-1, to=1-1]
    	\arrow["{\tau_A}"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
    	\arrow["{F'(\iota_{\rho(A)}^{\rho(C)})}"', from=2-2, to=1-2]
    	\arrow["{F(\iota_B^C)}", from=2-5, to=1-5]
    	\arrow["{\tau_B}"', from=2-5, to=2-6]
    	\arrow["{F'(\iota_{\rho(B)}^{\rho(C)})}"', from=2-6, to=1-6]
    \end{tikzcd}\]

    More precisely, \begin{align*}
(F'(\iota_{\rho(A)}^{\rho(C)}))(\tau_A(\alpha))= \tau_C(F(\iota_A^C)(\alpha))=\tau_C(F(\iota_B^C)(\beta)) =(F'(\iota_{\rho(B)}^{\rho(C)}))(\tau_B(\beta)).
    \end{align*}

title: Proposition
body_md: The group $B_{\vec{F}}$ and the group $\displaystyle \lim_{\longrightarrow}{}^{\vec{F}} Br$ are isomorphic.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cite[Proposition 4.6]{MR5118516}, the $\vec{F}$-equivariant direct limit $\displaystyle \lim_{\longrightarrow}{}^{\vec{F}} Br$ is isomorphic to $\displaystyle \lim_{\longrightarrow} Br \rtimes_{\phi} \vec{F}$, where $\displaystyle \lim_{\longrightarrow} Br$ is the regular direct limit, and $\phi: \vec{F} \to \textup{Aut}(\displaystyle \lim_{\longrightarrow} Br)$ is given by $\phi_f[P, \alpha] = [f(P), \alpha]$.

    Let $\sigma$ be the canonical generator of $Br_2$. It is easy to see that the direct limit $\displaystyle \lim_{\longrightarrow} Br$ is generated by the braid generators $\sigma_{ab} = [\{a, b\}, \sigma]$ for any two dyadic rationals $a<b$, with braid relations
    \begin{align*}
      &\sigma_{ab}\sigma_{cd}=\sigma_{cd}\sigma_{ab} \ \text{ if $(a-c)(a-d)(b-c)(b-d)>0$,} \\ 
      &\sigma_{ab}\sigma_{bc}=\sigma_{ac}\sigma_{ab}=\sigma_{bc}\sigma_{ac} \ \text{  for all $a,b,c$ with $a<b<c$}.\\ 
    \end{align*}
    
    The oriented Thompson group $\vec{F}$ is generated by $g_i$ for $i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$ with relations
    $$
    g_n g_l = g_l g_{n+2} \ \text{ for all $l < n$}
    $$

    The semidirect product $\displaystyle \lim_{\longrightarrow} Br \rtimes_{\phi} \vec{F}$ is generated by the union of the generating sets of its two factors. Its defining relations consist of the relations of both factors together with the following additional relations:
    $$
    g_i\sigma_{ab} = (\phi_{g_i}(\sigma_{ab}))g_i \ \text{ for all $i,a \text{ and } b$}
    $$

    Note that $\phi_{g_i}(\sigma_{ab}) = \sigma_{g_i(a) g_i(b)}$, so the generators and relations of $\displaystyle \lim_{\longrightarrow} Br \rtimes_{\phi} \vec{F}$ are the same as the generators and relations of $B_{\vec{F}}$.

\label{def: half grid diagram}
	A half grid diagram $\mathbb{H}$ is an $n \times 2n$ grid of squares, each of which is either empty or contains an $X$ or an $O$. We require that in each row there are exactly two nonempty squares, one containing an $X$ and the other containing an $O$, and each column has exactly one nonempty square (which may contain either an $X$ or an $O$).

title: Definition
body_md: Let $\mathbb{H}$ be an $n \times 2n$ half grid diagram. The $(0,2n)$-oriented tangle $\mathcal{T}(\mathbb{H})$ associated to $\mathbb{H}$ is defined by first connecting $X$ to $O$ in each row, then connecting each $X$ or $O$ to the bottom of the grid by vertical arcs, oriented upward in the case of an $X$ and downward in the case of an $O$. We again use the crossing convention that horizontal segments are always above vertical segments.

label: lem: iota is well defined
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem: iota is well defined}
    $\iota: \vec{F} \to B_{\vec{F}}$ is a well-defined map.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Given an element $g \in \vec{F}$, suppose that $(\mathcal{I}, \mathcal{J})$ and $(\mathcal{I}', \mathcal{J}')$ are two pairs of s.d. partitions representing $g$, we want to show that $[\mathcal{E}_+(\mathcal{J}), \mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}), g] = [\mathcal{E}_+(\mathcal{J}'), \mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}'}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}'}), g]$.
    
    Let $(\mathcal{I}'', \mathcal{J}'')$ be a common refinement of $(\mathcal{I}, \mathcal{J})$ and $(\mathcal{I}', \mathcal{J}')$. Note that the grid diagram $(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}''}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}'')}$ differs from $(\mathbb{H}_\mathcal{I}, \mathbb{H}_\mathcal{J})$ by adding some distant unlinked unknots lying above all other strands (Figure \ref{fig:adding-trivial-unknots-to-half-grids}). Hence after we turn $(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}''}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}''})$ into a braid $\mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}''}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}''})$, with some Reidemeister II moves, those distant unknots become trivial strands lying under all other strands (Figure \ref{fig:adding-trivial-strand-to-half-grids}). The same holds for $(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}'}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}'})$ and $(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}''}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}''})$. Moreover, by the procedure of turning the grid diagram into a braid (depicted in Figure \ref{fig:half-grid-pair-with-shift} and Figure \ref{fig:half-grid-braid-with-shift}) we see the refinement of the dyadic interval exactly corresponds to adding trivial strands on the dyadic braids. Thus, $[\mathcal{E}_+(\mathcal{J}), \mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}), g] = [\mathcal{E}_+(\mathcal{J}'), \mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}'}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}'}), g]=[\mathcal{E}_+(\mathcal{J}''), \mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}''}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}''}), g]$.

label: lem: iota preserves link
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem: iota preserves link}
    The map $\iota: \vec{F} \to B_{\vec{F}}$ satisfies $L(g)=\mathfrak{cl}(\iota(g))$ for all $g \in \vec{F}$. That is, $\iota$ preserves the link.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For any element $g \in \vec{F}$, let $(\mathcal{I}, \mathcal{J})$ be a pair of s.d. partitions representing $g$. Then
    $$
    \mathfrak{cl}(\iota(g)) = \mathfrak{cl}[\mathcal{E}_+(\mathcal{J}), \mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}), g] = [\textup{cl}(\mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}))] = [L(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}})]
    $$

    In the equation above we take classes of links in $C_0$. By Theorem \ref{thm: equivalent oriented links}, we have $[L(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}})] = [L(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J})]=L(g)$. Thus $L(g)=\mathfrak{cl}(\iota(g))$.
head: environment

label: thm: iota injective homomorphism
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm: iota injective homomorphism}
    $\iota: \vec{F} \to B_{\vec{F}}$ is an injective group homomorphism.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $\iota(g) = \iota(h)$, then $g = h$ by the definition of $\iota$ and Definition \ref{def: concentration on S_G}. Hence $\iota$ is injective.

    Next we prove that $\iota$ preserves the multiplication. Given $f, g \in \vec{F}$, to take the product of $g$ and $f$, we choose a s.d. partition pair $(\mathcal{I}, \mathcal{J})$ representing $f$, and a s.d. partition pair $(\mathcal{J}, \mathcal{K})$ representing $g$. Then $gf$ is represented by the s.d. partition pair $(\mathcal{I}, \mathcal{K})$. To show that $\iota(g) \iota(f) = \iota(gf)$, we just need to check that
    $$
    [\mathcal{E}_+(K), \mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{K}}), g][\mathcal{E}_+(J), \mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}), f] = [\mathcal{E}_+(K), \mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{K}}), gf]
    $$

    Note that $(\mathcal{E}_+(J), \mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}), f)$ is a morphism from $\mathcal{E}_+(\mathcal{I})$ to $\mathcal{E}_+(\mathcal{J})$, and $(\mathcal{E}_+(K), \mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{K}}), g)$ is a morphism from $\mathcal{E}_+(\mathcal{J})$ to $\mathcal{E}_+(\mathcal{K})$, we have
    $$
    [\mathcal{E}_+(K), \mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{K}}), g][\mathcal{E}_+(J), \mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}), f] = [\mathcal{E}_+(K), \mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{K}}) \mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}), gf]
    $$
    
    It remains to check that $\mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{K}}) \mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}) = \mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{K}})$. Indeed, after we turn $(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{K}})$ and $(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}})$ into the braids and concatenate them, the lower half of $\mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}})$ and the upper half of $\mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{K}})$ become mirrors to each other, and canceled by Reidemeister II moves (see Figure \ref{fig:half-grids-multiplication} for an example). Thus $\mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{K}}) \mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}) = \mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{K}})$.

title: Lemma
body_md: $TL(\iota_P^Q): TL_{|P|} \to TL_{|P|+1}$ is a well-defined map.
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Define the oriented dyadic Temperley-Lieb monoid $\overline{TL_{\vec{F}}}$ to be $\displaystyle \lim_{\longrightarrow}{}^{\vec{F}} TL$, the $\vec{F}$-equivariant direct limit of $TL$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Define the oriented dyadic Temperley-Lieb algebra $TL_{\vec{F}}$ to be the free $\mathbb{Z}$-module generated by the elements in $\overline{TL_{\vec{F}}}$, with the following linearity relation:
    $$
    a[P, \alpha, f] + b[P, \beta, f] \sim [P, a\alpha + b\beta, f]
    $$
    for any $[P, \alpha, f]$ and $[P, \beta, f]$ in $\overline{TL_{\vec{F}}}$, and any $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$. The multiplication on $TL_{\vec{F}}$ is induced by the multiplication in $\overline{TL_{\vec{F}}}$.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: $\tau$ is an $\vec{F}$-equivariant natural transformation.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first check that $\tau$ is indeed a natural transformation, that is, we check the following diagram commutes for any $P \leq Q$.
    \[\begin{tikzcd}
    	{Br_{|Q|}} & {TL_{|Q|}} \\
    	{Br_{|P|}} & {TL_{|P|}}
    	\arrow["{J_{|Q|}}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
    	\arrow["{Br(\iota_P^Q)}", from=2-1, to=1-1]
    	\arrow["{J_{|P|}}"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
    	\arrow["{TL(\iota_P^Q)}"', from=2-2, to=1-2]
    \end{tikzcd}\]
    
    For any $\alpha \in Br_{|P|}$, $(J_{|Q|} \circ Br(\iota_P^Q))(\alpha)$ is obtained by first adding trivial strands to $\alpha$ on $Q \setminus P$, then taking its Kauffman bracket. $(TL(\iota_P^Q) \circ J_{|P|})(\alpha)$ is obtained by first taking the Kauffman bracket of $\alpha$, then adding trivial strands on $Q \setminus P$, then taking Kauffman brackets again. Since taking Kauffman brackets doesn't depend on the order of crossings, the above diagram commutes.

    $\tau$ is $\vec{F}$-equivariant, because $\tau_P = J_{|P|} = J_{|g(P)|} = \tau_{g(P)}$ for any object $P$ and any $g\in \vec{F}$.
head: environment

label: def:jones-dyadic-braid-representation
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:jones-dyadic-braid-representation}
    Define $J_{\vec{F}}: B_{\vec{F}} \to TL_{\vec{F}}$ to be $i \circ id_\tau$. We say $J_{\vec{F}}$ is the Jones representation of $B_{\vec{F}}$.

label: thm:jones-dyadic-braid-representation-is-unitary
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:jones-dyadic-braid-representation-is-unitary}
    $J_{\vec{F}}$ is a unitary representation.
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

label: lem:braid-writhe-zero
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:braid-writhe-zero}
The braid $\mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}})$ has writhe $0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall we can view any grid diagram as a Legendrian link in the standard tight contact $S^3$. In \cite{MR2500576} and \cite[Proposition 4]{MR2602837}  we see that when turning a grid diagram into a braid contact geometrically, we are turning a Legendrian link into its transverse push-off. 
    
    Let $L(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}})$ be the Legendrian link corresponding to the grid $(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}})$, and let $T(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}})$ be the transverse push-off of $L(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}})$. It was shown in \cite[Proposition 5.7]{luo2024halfgriddiagramsthompson} that the Thurston-Bennequin number $tb(L(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}))=-n$, and the rotation number $rot(L(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}))=0$, where $2n$ is the size of the grid. Thus, according to \cite{MR2179261} we know the self-linking number $sl(T(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}))=tb(L(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}))-rot(L(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}}))=-n$. On the other hand, the braid $\mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}})$ represents $T(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}})$, so its writhe minus its number of strands equals the self-linking number, $-n$. Since the braid has $n$ strands, its writhe is zero.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Given $g \in \vec{F}$, let $(\mathcal{I}, \mathcal{J})$ be an s.d. $n$-partition pair representing $g$.
    
    By Lemma \ref{lem:braid-writhe-zero}, $\mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{I}}, \mathbb{H}_{\mathcal{J}})$ has writhe $0$. Hence
    \begin{align*}
    \langle J_{\vec{F}}(\iota(g))(\epsilon), \epsilon \rangle &= \frac{1}{(-A^2-A^{-2})^{|\mathcal{E}_+(\mathcal{J})|}} \langle cl(\mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_\mathcal{I}, \mathbb{H}_\mathcal{J})) \rangle(A) \\
    &= \frac{1}{(-A^2-A^{-2})^{|\mathcal{E}_+(\mathcal{J})|-1}} V_{\mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_\mathcal{I}, \mathbb{H}_\mathcal{J})}(A)
    \end{align*}

    On the other hand, we have Eq. \ref{equ: normalized Jones' polynomial for Thompson}:
    $$
    \langle \pi_J(g)(\xi), \xi \rangle = \frac{1}{(-A^2-A^{-2})^{n-1}}V_{L(\mathcal{I}, \mathcal{J})}(A)
    $$

    Recall that $cl(\mathfrak{b}(\mathbb{H}_\mathcal{I}, \mathbb{H}_\mathcal{J}))$ is isotopic to $L(\mathbb{H}_\mathcal{I}, \mathbb{H}_\mathcal{J})$, which is $L(\mathcal{I}, \mathcal{J})$ by Theorem \ref{thm: equivalent oriented links}. Note that $|\mathcal{E}_+(\mathcal{J})| = n$, then we have
    $$
    \langle \pi_J(g)(\xi), \xi \rangle = \langle J_{\vec{F}}(\iota(g))(\epsilon), \epsilon \rangle.
    $$

label: lem:upper-trees
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:upper-trees}
    For any finite sequence of signs $(\sigma_1, \sigma_2,\cdots, \sigma_n)$, there exists a tree $T$ with $n$ vertices $\{v_1<v_2<\cdots<v_n\}$ such that  $s(v_i)=\sigma_i$ for all $1 \leq i \leq n$ if $\sigma_1=+$, or $s(v_i)=-\sigma_i$ for all $i$ if $\sigma_1=-$.
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

label: lem:lower-tree
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:lower-tree}
    For any pair of dyadic numbers $a < b$, there exists a tree with vertices $v_1, v_2,..., v_n$ such that for some $1\leq i<j < n$, we have $v_i = a, v_j = b$. Moreover, we can assume that the tree satisfies $s(v_1) = +$, $s(v_2)=-$, $s(v_{i+1})=-s(v_i)$, and  $ s(v_{j+1})=-s(v_j)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We can easily find a s.d. partition containing breakpoints $a, b$, then consider the corresponding tree with vertices $v_1, v_2, ..., v_n$. Suppose that $v_i = a$ and $v_j = b$. Now we want to fix the signs of $v_2, v_{i+1}, v_{j+1}$.

    To realize that, we just need to add an extra vertex next to each of $v_1$,$v_i$, and $v_j$ lying on the right edge.
head: environment

label: prop:two-numbers-to-any-ab
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that $B_{\vec{F}}$ has braid generators $\sigma_{ab}$ for any two dyadic rational numbers $a,b$, and $\vec{F}$ generators $g_i$ for any nonnegative integer $i.$ We claim that $B_{\vec{F}}$ can be finitely generated by
    $$
    \sigma_{\frac{1}{4} \frac{1}{2}}, \sigma_{\frac{1}{2} \frac{3}{4}}, \sigma_{\frac{5}{8} \frac{3}{4}}, \sigma_{\frac{3}{4} \frac{7}{8}}, g_0, g_1, g_2
    $$
    
    We just need to show that any $\sigma_{ab}$ and $g_i$ can be generated by the above $7$ generators.

    By \cite{MR3565428}, $\vec{F}$ is isomorphic to the $3$rd Brown-Thompson group $F_3$, which has presentation
    $$
    \langle y_0, y_1, y_2, \cdots \mid y_n y_l = y_l y_{n+2}, \textup{for $l < n$} \rangle
    $$

    Note that these generators and relations are exactly the $\vec{F}$ generators $g_i$ and the $\vec{F}$ relations in Definition \ref{def:oriented-dyadic-braid-group}. Since $F_3$ can be generated by the first three generators $y_0, y_1, y_2$, any $\vec{F}$ generator $g_i$ can be generated by $g_0, g_1, g_2$.

    For any braid generator $\sigma_{ab}$ with $s(a)=s(b)=+$, there exists $f \in \vec{F}$ such that $f(\frac{1}{4})=a$ and $f(\frac{1}{2})=b$ by Proposition \ref{prop:two-numbers-to-any-ab}. From the previous argument, $f$ can be viewed as an element in $B_{\vec{F}}$ which can be generated by $g_0, g_1, g_2$. Hence, by the braid $\vec{F}$ relations, we have $\sigma_{ab} = \sigma_{f(\frac{1}{4})f(\frac{1}{2})} = f \sigma_{\frac{1}{4}\frac{1}{2}} f^{-1}$, so $\sigma_{ab}$ is generated by $g_0,g_1,g_2,\sigma_{\frac{1}{4}\frac{1}{2}}$.

    The proof is similar for $a, b$ with other sign combinations.
